## Proof

**Claim.** Yes. In fact, for *every* $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ there exists a sequence $\{x_n\}\subseteq X$ with $\|x_n\|\to 0$ and $Tx_n\to\alpha$. In particular this holds for $\alpha\neq 0$.

**Setup.** Since $T:X\to\mathbb{R}$ is a non-bounded (unbounded) linear operator on the normed space $X$,

$$\sup_{\|x\|=1}|Tx| \;=\; +\infty.$$

Hence there is a sequence $\{y_n\}\subseteq X$ with $\|y_n\|=1$ for all $n$ and $|Ty_n|\to\infty$.

**Extracting a signed divergent subsequence.** Since $|Ty_n|\to\infty$, at least one of the following holds along a subsequence: $Ty_n\to+\infty$ or $Ty_n\to-\infty$. Replacing $\{y_n\}$ by a subsequence and, if necessary, replacing each $y_n$ by $-y_n$ (which preserves $\|y_n\|=1$ and sends $Ty_n$ to $-Ty_n$), we may assume

$$Ty_n \;\longrightarrow\; +\infty.$$

In particular $Ty_n>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, so the construction below is well-defined; we discard the finitely many initial terms with $Ty_n\le 0$.

**Construction.** Fix an arbitrary $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and define

$$x_n \;=\; \frac{\alpha}{Ty_n}\, y_n.$$

**Verification.** By linearity of $T$,

$$Tx_n \;=\; \frac{\alpha}{Ty_n}\,T y_n \;=\; \alpha \qquad\text{for every } n,$$

so certainly $Tx_n\to\alpha$ (indeed the sequence is *constant* at $\alpha$). For the norms, using $\|y_n\|=1$ and $Ty_n\to+\infty$,

$$\|x_n\| \;=\; \frac{|\alpha|}{|Ty_n|}\,\|y_n\| \;=\; \frac{|\alpha|}{Ty_n} \;\longrightarrow\; 0.$$

Thus $\|x_n\|\to 0$ and $Tx_n\to\alpha$.

**Conclusion.** Such a sequence exists for *every* $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, and in particular for any nonzero $\alpha$. The key mechanism is that unboundedness of $T$ provides unit vectors $y_n$ with $|Ty_n|\to\infty$; rescaling $y_n$ by the (diverging) factor $\alpha/Ty_n$ drives the norm to $0$ while pinning the image exactly at $\alpha$. This is the hallmark behavior of an unbounded linear operator: it is *not* continuous at the origin, so it can send norm-null sequences to nonzero limits.
